text.p: Generations of mothers who admonished their children to wash their hands had the right idea for preventing infections, but too few people have gotten the message, doctors said Monday.

A surreptitious survey of 6,000 people in public restrooms in five cities, plus a phone survey of 1,000 more, revealed Americans do not wash their hands as often as they think and say they do, said Wirthlin Worldwide, an international research firm.

As a result, the American Society for Microbiology (ASM) and Bayer Pharmaceutical Divison launched a nationwide campaign Monday -- Operation Clean Hands -- to educate Americans on the health risks of not washing often enough or long enough with soap. The minimum should be 10-15 seconds of scrubbing, doctors said.

"Handwashing in this country is all but a lost art," said Dr. Michael Osterholm, chairman of the ASM committee on public health. In addition to spreading misery through colds and gastro-intentinal upsets, poor handwashing habits are more risky today because increasing numbers organisms are resistant to antibiotics.
Adults with minimal training in hygiene and indifferent teenagers working in mimimum wage positions at food outlets were major contributors to food-borne illnesses, he said.

Day care centres, particularly for infants and toddlers still in diapers, also pose a high risk. "Children's bottoms are bacterial, viral and parasitic uzis," he said. "All they need to set them off are unwashed human hands."

"Handwashing may seem trivial, but failing to do it can have tragic, even deadly, consequences," said Dr. Gail Cassell, ASM pubic and scientific affairs board chairman. Antibiotics have made Americans too complacent about infectious diseases, she said.

The survey revealed Chicagoans were the cleanest with 78 percent of bathroom users at Navy Pier washing their hands. At New York's Penn Station, only 60 percent headed for soap and water. At all the test sites, including San Francisco, Atlanta and New Orleans, women washed their hands more often than men.

In the phone interviews, 94 percent claimed they always washed after using the bathroom, 81 percent claimed to wash before handling or eating food and 78 percent said they washed after changing a diaper.
Most admitted they do not wash up after handling money, coughing, sneezing or petting an animal.
